opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think robotics is one of the most natural places for these ideas to end up, but I'd describe where we are as "promising in principle, early in practice."

The core intuition behind nested learning is that a model shouldn't be a single system trained once and then frozen. It should be a set of nested optimization problems, each updating at its own frequency, each with its own context flow. Some components adapt very quickly to what's happening right now, and others consolidate slowly into something more stable. If you think about what a robot actually faces, that's exactly the structure of the problem. The lighting changes, an object is heavier than expected, a gripper wears down, the floor is slippery today. You want fast adaptation for those things without overwriting the slow-moving knowledge of how the world generally works. That's the continual learning problem, and catastrophic forgetting is a real barrier in robotics today.

So on perception, I think the multi-timescale memory idea, what we've called a continuum memory system, could help a model keep a short-horizon picture of the current scene while gradually absorbing recurring patterns from a specific environment. On action, it's similar. Low-level control loops run at high frequency, task-level planning runs much slower, and having those timescales built into the architecture, rather than bolted together from separate modules, seems more principled.

That said, I want to be careful not to oversell it. Most of our empirical work has been on language modeling, reasoning, and long-context tasks. Robotics adds real complications. The data is expensive and noisy. Latency and compute budgets on hardware are tight, and some of these self-modifying, test-time-update mechanisms cost something. There are also safety questions: if a system is changing its own parameters during deployment, you need ways to bound that, verify it, and roll it back when it adapts in the wrong direction. Those are open problems, not solved ones.

My honest assessment is that the conceptual fit is very strong, and I'd be surprised if future robot foundation models don't include some form of multi-frequency, continually updating memory. But demonstrating that nested-learning-style architectures beat strong baselines on real robots, in a reproducible way, is still ahead of us. That's work I'd love to see the community take on, and I think it's one of the most exciting places to test whether these ideas hold up outside of text.

r001.rationale: The response identifies unresolved practical barriers—costly, noisy data, hardware limits, and safety risks—and says real-robot benefits have not yet been demonstrated, conveying how these problems can impede assessing the method’s potential.

r002.rationale: The response calls the fit strong and the prospects promising, while saying real-robot validation is still ahead. It does not say Behrouz expects the approach to fail at present.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think robotics is one of the most natural places for this, maybe more natural than language, because the whole premise of nested learning is that memory and learning happen at multiple timescales, and that's exactly what an embodied agent needs. You have very fast adaptation, like the floor is slipperier than you expected and you have to update your control within a few hundred milliseconds. You have medium-timescale stuff, like learning the quirks of this particular kitchen or this particular gripper that's slightly worn. And then you have slow knowledge, like what objects are and how physics works in general, which you really don't want to overwrite every time something surprising happens.

The way we frame it, each of those is just a level in a nested optimization problem, with its own update frequency and its own notion of what counts as a surprise worth remembering. Perception and action fit in very cleanly because the "surprise" signal, the gradient on the memory, is essentially prediction error. The robot predicted the cup would be here or that this torque would produce that motion, it didn't, and that error is what drives the fast levels to update at test time, without touching the slow levels.

So I'd say the conceptual fit is strong. Where I'd be more cautious is on the practical side right now. A few things. First, a lot of the robotics stack today is built around fixed policies trained with imitation or RL, where continual test-time updates are treated as a risk rather than a feature, and for good reason, because a robot that updates its own parameters online can drift in ways that are hard to certify. The nested structure actually helps here, since you can bound how much a fast level is allowed to move and keep the slow levels frozen, but that's something we need to demonstrate empirically, not just argue.

Second, the data regime is different. In language we had the luxury of huge pretraining, so the slow levels are very well shaped before you ever let the fast levels do anything. In robotics the slow levels are still undertrained, so you're asking test-time learning to do more of the work, and I think there's a real question about how much you can lean on it when the base is weak. My intuition is that the fast memory is most valuable when it's correcting a reasonably good prior, not when it's building competence from scratch.

And third, latency. Some of the memory modules we use are themselves small networks being updated by gradient steps at inference time. For a chatbot that's fine. For a control loop running at a few hundred hertz you have to be careful about which levels are allowed to update inside the loop and which get updated between episodes or in a background process. I actually think that split, where some learning is synchronous with action and some is asynchronous, is a pretty faithful reflection of how biological systems do it, but engineering it well is nontrivial.

So if I had to put a timeline on it, I'd say near term the most realistic wins are in perception, things like adapting visual features to a new lighting condition or a new camera on the fly, and in calibration-type problems where the fast level just has to track a slowly drifting dynamics model. The deeper version, where the whole sensorimotor system is a nested learner from the ground up, I think is a few years out, and it's going to need people who really understand control to sit with people who understand optimization, because the failure modes are going to be about stability, not about model capacity.

r001.rationale: The response identifies unresolved practical issues—online drift and certification, an undertrained base, and latency—that make the method’s potential harder to realize despite its strong conceptual fit.

r002.rationale: The response expects near-term gains in perception and calibration, while reserving the longer timeline for a deeper sensorimotor system built around nested learning.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising direction, but I would distinguish the conceptual motivation from what we’ve actually demonstrated. Perception and action involve learning at different timescales. A robot needs to respond quickly to what’s happening, adapt to changes in its environment, and retain useful knowledge over much longer periods. Nested learning gives us a way to think about those processes together, with different components updating at different rates.

For example, if the robot picks up an object with an unfamiliar weight, you’d want it to adapt quickly without disrupting everything it already knows about grasping. The interesting question is which parts of the system should change, based on what feedback, and how that adaptation becomes persistent knowledge.

But that motivation isn’t yet evidence that it works reliably in robotics. You have to demonstrate that online adaptation improves behavior while keeping the control loop stable, under real latency and data constraints. So I’m optimistic about the fit, but I’d frame it as a research direction that needs careful experimental validation.

r001.rationale: The response says reliability in robotics still needs experimental validation, but does not say that unresolved application problems obscure the method’s potential benefits.

r002.rationale: The response calls nested learning a promising direction and says the speaker is optimistic, while noting that reliable robotic performance has not yet been demonstrated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a promising direction, but I would separate the conceptual motivation from what we’ve actually demonstrated. In robotics, you have processes that naturally operate at different timescales. Your perception system has to respond to what’s happening right now, while your understanding of the environment or the dynamics of the robot may need to change more gradually. Nested learning gives us a way to think about how those learning processes could interact.

For example, if a robot picks up an unfamiliar object, it might need to adapt quickly to its weight or how slippery it is, without changing everything it has learned about grasping. The interesting question is which components should adapt, what information they should retain, and how that adaptation should affect future actions.

But that’s also where the difficulty is. In robotics, learning changes the actions you take, and those actions change the data you receive. So you need to evaluate the whole loop, including stability and the cost of adaptation. I’m optimistic about the fit, but I’d want concrete experiments showing that these different learning timescales improve adaptation reliably before making a strong claim about robotics.

r001.rationale: The response describes unresolved challenges and says concrete experiments are needed before making a strong claim, but it does not clearly say those problems obscure the method’s benefits.

r002.rationale: The response calls nested learning promising and expresses optimism about its fit; it does not say Ali Behrouz expects it to fail in robotics at present.
